<1>Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network?</1>
In platform-governed ecosystems, the conflict does not begin when the user decides to litigate, complain or formalize their dissatisfaction.<1>p. 780</1>
The user does not consume only access, utility, content or performance.<1>p. 781</1>
They consume an environment that presents itself as intelligible, assistive, responsive and, to some extent, worthy of practical credit.<1>p. 781</1>
On platforms, trust is not a spontaneous by-product of the good performance of the service.<1>p. 781</1>
Frequently, it is produced, calibrated and maintained by design.<1>p. 781</1>
This trust need not take the solemn form of an express guarantee to produce relevant legal effects.<1>p. 781</1>

It is enough that it acts stably upon the ordinary interpretation of the experience and upon the user's willingness to bear friction, accept vague justifications, normalize losses and remain in the cycle of use even when enjoyment has already been functionally degraded.<1>p. 781</1>
<1>Loss becomes routine.</1> In a service you use every day, small frustrations are gradually absorbed and stop looking like a problem. They start to look like the normal workings of the system.

<1>Friction gets another name.</1> What could be read as a failure or an abuse appears as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, a security measure, a necessary update or a simple step of use.

<1>Customer service listens but does not solve.</1> Friendly messages, answers that seem to explain and service circuits built to receive the complaint without reconstructing the problem gradually drain your strength to contest.
Loss no longer appears as an exceptional event and comes to be metabolized as part of the normal functioning of the system.<1>p. 781</1>

Instead of promptly triggering a reading of inadequacy or abusiveness, it may be reconfigured by the platform as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, an understandable inconvenience, a security measure, a necessary update or a simple step of use.<1>p. 781</1>

Persona, operational cordiality, messages of closeness, excessively reassuring simplifications, answers of explanatory appearance and service circuits designed to absorb dissatisfaction without effective reconstruction of the problem may operate, together, as a technique of demobilization.<1>p. 782</1>
The conflict does not disappear.<1>p. 782</1>
It is governed in its pre-legal phase, through mechanisms that turn loss into tolerable noise, opacity into normality and asymmetry into absorbable experience.<1>p. 782</1>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it grows, because trust itself is used to lower your resistance. The platform produces enough signs of clarity and care for you to settle in, even when what you use has already been harmed.
The central vulnerability of this subtype is, once again, semiotic vulnerability, but now intensified by the management of trust as a way of modulating resistance.<1>p. 782</1>
They face an ecosystem that produces signs of intelligibility and care sufficient to induce accommodation, even when the materiality of enjoyment has already been compromised.<1>p. 782</1>
Rumor, in this context, does not remain mere noise external to the supply.<1>p. 784</1>

One does not buy only the available object. One also buys on account of the anticipated object, the sensed event, the awaited skin, the imagined update. The future comes to organize the present of consumption.<1>p. 785</1>

When content circulates without official confirmation, the platform preserves a margin of plausible deniability and strategic flexibility to reshape schedules, alter products, recalibrate offers or simply harvest reactions without fully assuming, in its communication, what was anticipated.<1>p. 784</1>

It is not a matter of imposing an impracticable duty to prevent every rumor, every leak or every community speculation. Nor is it a matter of turning the company into a universal certifier of rumors.<1>p. 786</1>

It lies in recognizing that, once a specific, repeated expectation materially capable of guiding consumption decisions is installed in the ecosystem, the platform no longer remains in a neutral position.<1>p. 785</1>

<1>Hypercuratorial anticipation.</1> It is the way the platform governs what you expect from the future of the game. It does not act only through announcements, trailers and seasons. It may also act through rumors organized by third parties, which the company tolerates because they keep the community attentive and ready to spend.
Hypercuratorial anticipation, already delimited as a mechanism of governance of the present and the future of enjoyment, takes on a specific form here.<1>p. 784</1>

It may also operate through unofficial circuits of curated rumor, in which partial images, technical references, fragmentary leaks, presumed calendars and speculations deemed plausible are organized by leakers, influencers and channels specialized in narratives of a consumable future.<1>p. 784</1>
<1>Silence in the face of an expectation that already moves the community.</1> The company keeps quiet or answers evasively about something that is already guiding players' planning.

<1>The denial that later falls apart.</1> The company denies something specific and later does practically the same thing. This contradiction between what it said and what it did may weigh when the question is whether there was deception.
<1>The expectation confirmed and then frustrated.</1> The company confirms or feeds the expectation and then does not deliver, without a proportionate explanation.
In this hypothesis, the contradiction between communication and conduct may acquire its own relevance for the examination of deceptiveness and of legitimately formed trust.<1>p. 786</1>

In all these situations, the point is not to punish the mutability inherent in continuous digital services, but to prevent their structural flexibility from being converted into communicational immunity.<1>p. 786</1>
<1>Thinking only the contract counts.</1> The way the company talks to you also produces effects, and not only the clauses and formal acts.
<1>Thinking trust is only your own feeling.</1> Trust, here, is something the environment organizes, and not a private impression.
<1>Thinking the conflict only begins when you complain outside the platform.</1> The platform may govern precisely the moment when you realize you have lost something.
The first is the tendency to consider the discursive dimension of supply irrelevant, as if only clauses and formal acts produced legal effects.<1>p. 783</1>
The second is the tendency to treat trust as the user's private feeling, and not as a functional arrangement of the environment.<1>p. 783</1>

[...] a duty of clarification, non-contradiction and justification when ecosystemically relevant rumors, endowed with sufficient social credibility and functionally capable of influencing spending plans, purchase priority or waiting for enjoyment, are the object of specific prompting by users or become persistently integrated into the consumption environment.<1>p. 786</1>
Omission, in this framework, ceases to be a mere neutral communicational choice and may come to be a relevant informational insufficiency in a context of operative expectation.<1>p. 786</1>
The legal response compatible with this framework tends to require more than mere retrospective reparation.<1>p. 783</1>
It is enough to manage the way it is perceived.<1>p. 783</1>
In many environments, the platform does not need to formally prevent the conflict in order to reduce it.<1>p. 783</1>

<1>Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network?</1><2>Infrastructure and intermediation IOCs</2>
The market, the offer and even the social relevance of what circulates within it reach the consumer and the user through private filters of visibility, salience and intelligibility.<1>p. 761</1>

The incidence of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption on infrastructure and intermediation platforms is not defined by the final object traded nor by the traditional economic classification of the sector in which the platform operates.<1>p. 760</1>

In their formal language, they frequently appear as neutral spaces of encounter between seller and buyer, between sender and receiver, between advertiser and audience, between content producers and the public.<1>p. 761</1>
This description, although partially true on a superficial level, is insufficient to capture the real structure of supply.<1>p. 761</1>
They consume, before that, private frames that define what will be seen as more relevant, more reliable, more comparable, safer, more popular or more worthy of attention.<1>p. 761</1>

<1>In online stores.</1> The terms of use of the large marketplaces show that the platform organizes much more than listings. It handles the rules, visibility, payment, reputation, delivery and dispute resolution.
<1>On social networks.</1> The terms of the large networks show private rules about what stays up, who sees what, what is moderated and how conversation circulates.
In both cases, the platform does not merely host listings. It administers criteria of presentation, trust, prioritization and legibility of the market accessible to the consumer.<1>p. 762</1>

Here too the platform does not merely “let appear” content produced by third parties. It administers the way this content enters the user's field of perception and how its relevance is socially stabilized.<1>p. 762</1>
In both cases, the platform governs the environment of appearance.<1>p. 762</1>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it grows because the platform's screen comes to manufacture what is real for you, and what it does not show almost ceases to exist.
It is a semiotic vulnerability intensified by structural dependence on the interface as producer of the accessible real.<1>p. 763</1>

In environments like these, the supplier's promise lies not only in the explicit discourse of neutrality, efficiency or convenience. It lies also in the implicit promise of intelligibility of the market or of social circulation.<1>p. 763</1>

When this intelligibility is governed by opaque criteria, non-transparent internal interests or non-auditable patterns of ranking, enjoyment comes to be affected in its very core of legibility.<1>p. 763</1>

This includes, depending on the case, the form of presentation of offers, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of ratings and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the signs of reliability provided by the interface, the context in which content appears, the relevant moderation criteria and the mechanisms by which the platform induces a perception of market, consensus or priority.<1>p. 763</1>
<1>Thinking the screen is just decoration.</1> The way things are shown is part of what the platform supplies.
<1>Thinking the platform is only liable for what it wrote.</1> What it actually does with visibility also counts, and not only what is in the contract or the advertising.
<1>Thinking the problem is only the last step.</1> The failed purchase or the removed post is the end of a story. What led there was the storefront the platform set up.

The second is the tendency to imagine that the platform would be legally liable only for what it expressly said in a clause or in advertising, as if the effective governance of visibility were legally irrelevant.<1>p. 763</1>

The third is the tendency to reduce the dispute to the terminal act, such as the failed purchase, the removal of a piece of content or the supposed preference for a given offer, without investigating the private structure of salience that conditioned the user's entire experience.<1>p. 763</1>

What is demanded is sufficient intelligibility to understand how the environment organizes the user's experience and how certain choices of the platform interfere in the formation of expectation, in the comparability between alternatives and in the possibility of contestation.<1>p. 764</1>

This may occur both in e-commerce and in the social circulation of content, whenever the platform substantially alters the functional role of the infrastructure it offered as an environment of exchange, reach or recognition.<1>p. 764</1>

The subtype thus shows that the infrastructure and intermediation platform is not a mere neutral corridor through which previously formed wills circulate. It is an agent in the construction of the field in which these wills become possible, perceptible and operable.<1>p. 764</1>

In this family, the central utility is not limited to the final payment for a ride, delivery or completed task.<1>p. 765</1>
The object enjoyed, here, is neither a static good nor a simple service rendered externally to the worker.<1>p. 765</1>
It is a governed productive environment, without which everyday economic activity does not become viable on the terms in which the platform itself promised and structured it.<1>p. 765</1>

The instruments deployed by iFood, 99Food, Uber and 99 insist, with variations of language, on characterizing the partners as independent, on presenting the platform as an environment of technological intermediation and on ruling out any hierarchical bond or mandatory exclusivity.<1>p. 765</1>

It is a matter of recognizing that the functional utility indispensable to the exercise of economic activity is offered, modulated and reconfigured by a private architecture that the subject does not control.<1>p. 766</1>
The focus, for the purposes of this typology, is on the regime of supply.<1>p. 766</1>
This incidence does not dissolve the subtype into undifferentiated labor law, but neither does it allow itself to be neutralized by contractual self-descriptions of formal autonomy.<1>p. 768</1>

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it is sharper, because you depend on the app not only to receive requests but also to understand your position, your risk and your earnings.
It is a semiotic vulnerability associated with productive dependence.<1>p. 766</1>

It is a semiotic regime that organizes the subject's economic experience and redistributes onto them the costs of interpreting an environment whose material functioning they cannot audit autonomously.<1>p. 766</1>
<1>When the distribution of requests changes without explanation.</1> Rides or deliveries become scarce, and you do not know whether it was demand, your rating or a new rule.
<1>When the payment calculation changes.</1> The same work starts to earn less, and the parameters that would explain the difference stay hidden.
<1>When the restriction or the block arrives.</1> The account is limited or deactivated, and you cannot link the penalty to a cause you can check.
<1>When the account stays active but is worth less.</1> The program's name and the look of the partnership stay the same, but what justified your being there has been emptied out.

Opacity about the distribution of opportunities, about prioritization criteria, about parameters of variable pay, about the effects of ratings and about the causality of restrictions falls, in this context, not only on abstract contractual comfort, but on the very material conditions of life of subjects who depend on this environment to work.<1>p. 767</1>
<1>Thinking lower earnings are just a risk of the job.</1> The drop may come from a rule change made by the app without explanation.
<1>Looking only at the final penalty.</1> The block is usually the end of a story of targets, incentives and threats, and that story counts too.
<1>Thinking the lack of clarity is just how technology is.</1> Hiding the metrics and criteria is not inevitable, and it is precisely part of the problem.
The second is to treat the final sanction as an isolated event, without reconstructing the regime of conduct, incentive and threat that preceded it.<1>p. 768</1>
The third is to accept the lack of transparency about metrics and criteria as an inevitable consequence of technology, when precisely this opacity is part of the central legal problem.<1>p. 768</1>

Relevant rule changes, changes in calculation, reconfigurations of priority, redefinitions of metrics or sanctions with material impact cannot be shielded by a generic discourse of efficiency, security or algorithmic optimization. They must be made minimally verifiable.<1>p. 767</1>
This does not mean opening the system entirely, nor turning the Judiciary into the platform's technical administrator.<1>p. 767</1>
Without this minimum, the platform simultaneously concentrates the power to organize economic activity and the power to make opaque the facts needed to contest it.<1>p. 767</1>
Enjoyment, therefore, is the productive enjoyment of a governed environment. The platform worker consumes the very infrastructure that makes them economically operative.<1>p. 766</1>
